slides: Open by locating Cayley graphs as the first durable bridge from algebra to geometry. The audience should hear that the chapter is not merely drawing groups; it is choosing a generating set, turning multiplication into motion, and then asking which geometric features survive beyond the chosen picture.

Use the route slide as a contract for the lecture. Each stop adds one layer of structure: graph notation, generator-colored Cayley edges, graph distance, cycles from relations, free reduction, and finally the small list of invariants that the notebook checks computationally.

Begin with ordinary graph language before adding group structure. A vertex is an object, an edge records adjacency, orientation records direction when needed, and a label records the move type. The important habit is to read a diagram as data, not as decoration.

Present the Cayley construction as a repeated local rule. From every group element g and every generator s, draw the same colored move from g to gs. This makes the graph homogeneous: the view from any vertex is a translated copy of the view from the identity.

Pause on the generator colors in the grid because they encode the chosen generating set. A blue horizontal step and a teal vertical step commute, so the square loop is not an accident of the drawing. It is the visible trace of the relation ab equals ba.

Introduce the word metric as graph distance from the identity. The ball of radius n is the part reachable by at most n generator steps, and the sphere is the new frontier at exactly n steps. Stress that the metric depends on the selected generators.

Use the comparison to separate two sources of geometry. The grid has square cycles because the generators commute, while the free case branches without closing up. Relations are therefore geometric evidence: they identify different words that end at the same vertex.

Reduced words are the syntax that keeps the free group tree from immediately folding back on itself. After writing a letter, the inverse letter is forbidden as the next outward step. That simple local rule creates unique geodesics back to the identity.

Read the rooted tree from the identity outward. The root has four choices for a, a inverse, b, and b inverse; every later vertex has one edge back toward a shorter word and three outward choices. This is the visual reason the free-group ball is a tree.

The commutator path is a useful diagnostic because the same word behaves differently in different groups. In the grid it closes up, recording commutativity. In the free group it remains a nontrivial reduced word, so the path ends away from the identity.

Turn distance shells into numbers. The grid spheres grow linearly in the infinite model, while the free group spheres multiply by three after the first step. These counts are not yet the full growth theory, but they prepare the later invariant vocabulary.

This slide names the graph checks that make a Cayley picture mathematically inspectable. Degree at the identity, connectedness, cycle behavior, tree status, sphere counts, and sampled hyperbolicity each test a visible claim rather than trusting the image by eye.

Warn students about finite windows. A rendered ball has an artificial boundary where the drawing stops, so edge vertices look incomplete. The durable information is the pattern that remains stable as the radius grows: local labels, forced cycles, branching rules, and distance counts.

Use the exercise as a live prediction task. Students should first name the generators, then predict a visible feature before computing: a relation should close a loop, a free generator should add branching, and adding inverses should make graph distance symmetric.

Close by returning to the chapter question. A Cayley graph remembers multiplication by generators, word length, relations as cycles, and large-scale branching. It intentionally forgets the spelling of words once two spellings represent the same group element.
